guest.3:
10-MINUTE GUEST SPOT (advisor dinner seminar). The host has introduced you, so skip your bio. [About 1 minute.]

Thank you, [Host]. Before I say anything else: everyone has food in front of them, so let's use it. Take one bite of whatever is on your plate. Don't change a thing. Chew the way you always do, and count every chew silently until you swallow. [Pause and let the room chew.] How many? [Take two or three answers; most people land between 10 and 15.]
guest.4: [About 30 seconds.] Most people chew 10 to 15 times. Try 32 for the rest of dinner, and put your fork down between bites. You'll eat less without trying, because fullness signals take about twenty minutes to arrive. That's the smallest habit I know. And it matters for a much bigger reason than your waistline.
guest.15: [About 45 seconds.] Here's the bigger reason. Alzheimer's shows up late, but it starts in midlife. According to the Alzheimer's Association, changes in the brain can begin 20 years or more before the first symptom. So the window to lower your odds isn't at 75. It's now.
guest.23: [About 30 seconds.] Raise your hand if you have a retirement plan. [Most hands go up.] Now keep it up if that plan covers ten years of memory care. [Most hands go down.] That's the uninsured decade.
guest.24: [About 1 minute.] A 2025 study in Nature Medicine put the lifetime risk of dementia after age 55 at 42 percent: 35 percent for men, 48 percent for women. For a couple, roughly two in three that it reaches at least one of you. One honest caveat: that counts all dementia, including mild late-life cases that never need a facility. You insured the house against fire. You did not insure the likelier thing.
guest.25: [Optional, about 30 seconds; skip if the host asked you to keep it short.] The house burns: your carrier pays. A wreck: your carrier. You die early: life insurance. You can't work: disability. A hospital stay: health insurance. Ten years of dementia care? You do.
guest.26:
[About 1 minute.] And here's the part that surprises every room: Medicare pays zero toward custodial care. Memory care, in-home aides, assisted living: it's private pay until you've spent down to Medicaid. Long-term-care insurance used to be the answer, but very few carriers still sell new standalone policies, and many policyholders have seen steep rate increases.

[If the host sells annuities or long-term-care hybrid products, replace that last sentence with: 'Funding this risk is exactly what [Host] and their team help families do.']
guest.27: [About 1 minute.] Here's one realistic decade after a diagnosis at 70. The early years, about 35 to 40 thousand dollars. The middle years, with a paid caregiver and adult day care, about 170 to 180 thousand. The last years, 24/7 care, about 290 to 340 thousand. Roughly half a million dollars. The Alzheimer's Association's own average is about $405,000 per person, and 70 percent of it comes from the family.
guest.29:
[About 1.5 minutes.] So here's the reframe. A policy can help fund this risk, and that's the conversation [Host] is here to have with you tonight. But a policy can't lower the risk itself. That part is on you: about ten hours a month on the habits the research links to better odds. Nothing prevents dementia outright, and I'll never tell you it does. But it's the only premium that pays before the claim: better sleep, strength and energy, often within about six weeks.

Want your own number? The calculator on this slide prices a decade of care in your state, and you can send the result straight to [Host].
guest.close:
[About 1 minute.] One thing tonight: if you'd like your own picture, the free MindSpan assessment is on the screen. About seven minutes on your phone. [If the host bought books: 'And there's a copy of The Uninsured Decade at your seat.'] Nothing I've said tonight is for sale.

Begin with the end in mind. Don't lose your identity and your dignity while you still have a choice. [Host], thank you for having me. [Hand back to the host. Total: about 10 minutes.]

evening.5: ADVISOR CLIENT EVENING (~35 minutes, then the host's 5). Keep the intro to 30 seconds; the host has usually introduced you. Thirty years in practice; founder of My4MLife; three books. One honest line for the record: tonight is education, not medical, financial or legal advice. The why comes on the next slide.
evening.13: Pause here. Let it land. … Why does any of this matter? Losing a few pounds is nice. But it's not why I do this work. It matters because of how it ends. Remember the end I told you about at the start: don't lose your identity and your dignity while you still have a choice. [Advisor edition: the 4M overview and the quick check-in are cut for time; go straight into the Brain section.]
evening.34: Thank you. Take two or three general questions; anything personal or medical goes to the free care-coordinator call. Then: 'Tonight you heard the health half of the answer. [Host] has the other half.' Advance to the next slide and hand off.
evening.host: Hand off: 'The legal and financial half of the answer belongs to [Host], and it has deadlines: powers of attorney, health-care directives, and a look at what your plan and your policies already cover. [Host], thank you for filling this room.' Sit down and leave this slide up while the host speaks (about 5 minutes). Then come back up for the drawing.
